label: Columbia
rationale: The record that answers the charge that the early 1950s were Ellington's 'off period'. Its centerpiece, 'A Tone Parallel to Harlem', is the strongest case in the catalogue for Ellington as a large-form composer: John Edward Hasse writes that Harlem is 'regarded by a number of observers (including, reportedly, the composer himself) as Ellington's best extended work' and quotes it called 'every bit as much a miniature masterpiece as is Rhapsody in Blue'; Ted Gioia calls it 'a masterpiece by almost any measure' (both quoted in S1). Consensus across independent listing traditions is warm but not unanimous, and both sides are recorded here: AllMusic 4.5/5 (Scott Yanow: 'One of the great Duke Ellington sets'), the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4/5, and the Penguin Guide 3.5/4 — with Tom Hull in the Village Voice dissenting ('Hodges-less, coming out of his most pretentious composerly period, scratching and kicking to hang on'), all as tabulated in S1. Session gravity is the second argument: the 1951-52 orchestra is the transitional band that carried the canon from the Blanton-Webster era to the 1956 Newport breakthrough — Clark Terry, Cat Anderson, Willie Smith, Paul Gonsalves, Harry Carney, Juan Tizol, and Louie Bellson, whose 'Skin Deep' is the drum feature that made his name (S1, S3, and the Fresno provenance reported by KVPR in the search trail). Discovery value: Columbia took the record seriously enough to issue it on its classical Masterworks line (S2 review). It is also the canon's missing hinge — the record immediately before 'Ellington at Newport' (already included, 1956) in the band's own arc.

personnel_record.notes: Original five-track LP programme only (Columbia ML 4639, 1953). The later 13-track editions add 'The Controversial Suite' (recorded 1951-12-11) and 'The Liberian Suite' (1947 sessions, one source places part of it at Liederkranz Hall, New York) — excluded here as reissue-only additions, so this record describes four sessions across two rooms. Producer: George Avakian for tracks 2-5 (S2, S3); track 1 'Skin Deep' was produced by Duke and Mercer Ellington and recorded by Bert Porter at a Fresno dance date (S3). No source consulted documents the session engineer for tracks 2-5, so engineer is null rather than inferred; the Larry Keyes 'Engineer, Digital Restoration' credit on S3 belongs to the 1987 CD master, not the 1951-52 sessions. Year: 1953 is the release year (S1 infobox, S2, S3, S5). Conflict recorded: the Wikipedia Ellington discography table dates the album 1952 with 'year recorded 1952'. Venue conflict recorded: S1 says only 'recorded in New York' for tracks 2-7, while S3 names Columbia 30th Street Studio per track — the more specific claim is used and marked obs. Bass: S1's list also names Oscar Pettiford with no track attribution; S2 and S3 name Wendell Marshall alone, and Marshall was the band's bassist through this period, so Pettiford is omitted — flagged here rather than silently dropped. Johnny Hodges is kept at unk for the reason given on his personnel entry. LP sides are not documented in the sources consulted (the original-release track order is), so side is null throughout rather than reconstructed. Style: style_primary 'post-bop' follows the canon's existing coding of its other Ellington rows (Ellington at Newport, Such Sweet Thunder, ...And His Mother Called Him Bill); AllMusic files the album under Big Band and Swing.

scope_check.boundary_note: The 1951–1952 recordings and 1953 release clear the date gate. AllMusic classifies the music as Big Band and Swing (S2), not the dossier's post-bop; the references differ on whether this represents a meaningful stretch from the canon's bebop/post-bebop center, though neither treats it as excluded.

ballot.case_for: The strongest claim is a defining compositional statement: Hasse reports assessments of 'A Tone Parallel to Harlem' as Ellington's finest extended work, while Gioia calls it 'a masterpiece by almost any measure' (both quoted through S1). Support extends beyond that centerpiece: AllMusic awards 4.5/5, Penguin 3.5/4, and Rolling Stone 4/5, with Yanow calling the album 'One of the great Duke Ellington sets' (S1). The transitional orchestra connects directly to the personnel world of the already-canonized Newport band, while Bellson's 'Skin Deep' and Betty Roché's extended 'Take the "A" Train' give listeners immediate routes into its orchestral power and individual voices (S1–S3).
ballot.case_against: The evidence establishes strong reviews more securely than indispensable canon status: the dossier supplies no demonstrated Core Collection designation or comparable canon-list convergence, and Hull's dissent directly challenges the composerly ambition on which the strongest claim rests (S1). The original five-track LP combines a live drum showcase, expanded older repertoire, and a studio tone poem across four sessions, making its claim as a unified, load-bearing statement less secure than the stature of 'Harlem' alone. Its swing-centered idiom requires an affirmative connection to this canon's center, and most reception evidence remains mediated through Wikipedia, with unresolved personnel attributions further limiting confidence in the dossier.
ballot.disagreement: Reference 1 judges the defining work, favorable guide ratings, and Newport personnel bridge sufficient for consensus_core/strong, treating the stylistic labeling issue as non-gating. Reference 2 favors contested/consider, giving greater weight to the swing/post-bop tension, limited demonstrated canon-list consensus, and secondary sourcing; it nevertheless identifies strong as defensible if 'Harlem' receives greater weight.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give the original five-track album strong-priority listening consideration, with 'Harlem' as its decisive claim and the swing-lineage fit left for his judgment.
